title: Carr, Colorado Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Carr wells have a 300-foot median depth, with finished well costs commonly modeled at $16,500-$28,500.
h1: What Carr, Colorado Wells Are Really Like
intro_html:
Buying land near Carr means evaluating the well as part of the property, not treating it as a minor utility detail. Records within five miles show a wide range of drilling depths, but the typical well is about 300 feet deep. Most reported wells produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, which is a useful range for ordinary household planning.

The records also show why a nearby permit is only a starting point. Carr sits on plains terrain with alluvium and sedimentary rock, and permits commonly identify an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer. Before closing on land or pricing a new build, compare nearby well depths, water levels, construction details, and intended use with the specific lot.

sections.heading: Carr well depth depends on the local formation
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Carr is 300 feet. The middle half runs from 150 to 497 feet, so a driller bidding a new well should not rely on the median alone. Many wells fall well below or above it. The 90th-percentile depth is 612 feet, and the deepest record reaches 880 feet.

Depth records are spread across the area: 14% are under 100 feet, 34% are from 100 to 300 feet, 41% are from 300 to 600 feet, and 11% reach 600 feet or more. Carr’s alluvium and plains sedimentary rock can produce different drilling conditions from one parcel to the next. Nearby records around Nunn and Wellington can provide useful comparisons, but they do not guarantee the same depth on your lot.

sections.heading: Carr well yields usually support normal household use
sections.html:
Among Carr-area records that report pump yield, the median is 11.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 10.0 and 12.0 gallons per minute. That is a solid reported result for typical household demand, but a yield test is still needed for a particular well and property.

The distribution is concentrated: 85% of reported wells produce from 5 to 15 gallons per minute, while 15% report more than 15 gallons per minute. No reported wells fall under 1 gallon per minute or between 1 and 5 gallons per minute in this dataset. These figures describe tested or reported wells, not a promise for an unbuilt well. Ask for the permit, pump test, storage setup, and intended domestic or stock use.

sections.heading: Carr water levels show a shallower recent measurement
sections.html:
The median static water level near Carr is 80 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 58 to 100 feet. That matters for pump selection, trench planning, and evaluating how much lift the system must handle. It is also different from total well depth: a 300-foot well may encounter usable water substantially above the bottom.

By measurement decade, the median depth to water was 100 feet in the 2010s and 70 feet in the 2020s. That series points to a shallower measured water level in the newer records, not a dropping water table. The records are a mixed collection of wells and measurement dates, so a buyer should still obtain the current static level for the actual well and ask how it changes during pumping.

sections.heading: Carr’s permit history shows steady local well use
sections.html:
Colorado DWR records contain 510 permitted wells within five miles of Carr. Of those, 347 are recorded as constructed, 365 report total depth, 204 report pump yield, and 114 report static water level. The missing fields are important: a map point without construction or test details cannot answer every question about a property.

Permit activity was strongest in the 2000s, with 170 permits, followed by 108 in the 2010s and 75 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025. The most active drillers in these records are Crandall Drilling & Pump Service, including Crandall Jr. and Howard H., with 91 records; Ingram Drilling Inc., including Stephen E. Ingram, with 60; and Glenn A. Clement, with 40. Past activity does not establish current availability or pricing.

sections.heading: What a new Carr well may cost
sections.html:
The local drilling model uses $35 to $55 per foot for alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. At the 300-foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole at about $10,500 to $16,500. A finished system, including pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work, is modeled at about $16,500 to $28,500.

Those figures are planning ranges, not a guaranteed bid. A deeper-than-median hole can move the drilling portion higher, and access, casing, grout, water testing, electrical distance, and difficult ground can affect the final scope. Have a driller price the anticipated depth range rather than asking only for a per-foot rate. Confirm what is included in the finished-well number before comparing bids.

sections.heading: Check Carr water quality, yield, and septic constraints
sections.html:
Sixteen PFAS sampling or contamination sites are mapped within about 10 miles of Carr. The area also has six historic mine features and one EPA Superfund or cleanup site. These mapped sites do not prove that a particular well is contaminated, but they are a reason to review site history, well location, and laboratory water tests before buying.

Low yield and dry-hole risk cannot be ruled out by a strong area median. Confirm the well’s construction report, casing and grout details, pump test, static water level, and actual water chemistry. For a new home, septic setbacks, drainfield space, driveway access, and the proposed building envelope need to work together. An exempt household-use well still has Colorado limits, including the 35 gallons-per-minute pumping limit, and an over-appropriated basin may require an augmentation plan.

sections.heading: Do the Carr well work before you buy or build
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel and compare surrounding permits, not just the closest well symbol. Records near Nunn, Wellington, Pierce, and Ault can help show regional patterns, while the Carr-area results remain the better guide. Pay particular attention to wells with reported depth, yield, static level, and construction information.

For an existing property, make the sale contingent on reviewing the permit and having the well and pump inspected. Request a current flow or recovery test and certified water testing, especially where environmental sites are nearby. For vacant land, get a written drilling proposal, confirm equipment access, locate the future septic and house areas, and verify the intended water use with Colorado DWR. A nearby successful well improves your information; it does not guarantee success on a different lot.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Carr, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within five miles of Carr is 300 feet. The middle half ranges from 150 to 497 feet, while the 90th-percentile depth is 612 feet and the deepest record is 880 feet. For budgeting, ask a driller to price a depth range rather than assuming every Carr well will be 300 feet.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Carr, Colorado?
faq.a: The local model uses $35 to $55 per foot. At the 300-foot median depth, the drilled hole is modeled at about $10,500 to $16,500. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $16,500 to $28,500. Actual bids depend on depth, access, construction, and included equipment.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Carr?
faq.a: Reported Carr-area wells have a median yield of 11.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 10.0 to 12.0 gallons per minute. Eighty-five percent of reported yields are from 5 to 15 gallons per minute, and 15% exceed 15 gallons per minute. A property-specific pump or recovery test remains necessary.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Carr, Colorado?
faq.a: The area has 16 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles, along with historic mine features and an EPA Superfund or cleanup site. Those records do not determine water quality at a specific address. Test the actual well through a qualified laboratory and review site history before using the water for drinking.

faq.q: What should I check before buying a property with a Carr well?
faq.a: Review the Colorado DWR permit, construction report, total depth, pump yield, static water level, casing and grout details, and recent water tests. The area median static level is 80 feet below surface, but each well differs. Also confirm septic space, access, intended household or stock use, and any need for an augmentation plan.
